                    ### Question
                    A 40-year-old male visits a urologist and reports that for the past 2 weeks, his penis has been gradually curving to the right with associated pain during intercourse. He is able to have a normal erection and he does not recollect of any trauma to his penis. Although he is married, he admits to having unprotected sexual relationship with several females in the past year. His vitals are normal and physical examination in unremarkable except for a lesionless curved penis. It is painless to touch. Test results for sexually transmitted disease is pending. Which of the following is the most likely cause?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Fibrosis of corpus cavernosa
opb. Congenital hypospadias
opc. Syphilitic chancre
opd. Fibrosis of tunica albuginea
ope. Hypertrophy of corpus cavernosa

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The most likely cause of the patient's symptoms, including the gradual curvature of the penis and pain during intercourse without recollection of trauma, is Peyronie's disease. This condition is characterized by fibrosis of the tunica albuginea, which aligns with the patient's presentation of a curved penis that is painless to touch. The retrieved evidence path that links fibrosis and Peyronie's disease to the tunica albuginea supports this diagnosis. Other options such as syphilitic chancre and congenital hypospadias are less likely due to the absence of lesions and the late onset of symptoms, respectively. Hypertrophy of the corpus cavernosa is also unlikely as there is no evidence of hypertrophy on physical examination. Therefore, the diagnosis of Peyronie's disease, supported by the evidence of fibrosis causing this condition in the tunica albuginea, is the most consistent with the patient's clinical presentation and available evidence.
